name: Henry Gurney
geography: West Barsham Hall, Norfolk; Great Ellingham, Norfolk
summary: 'Last Gurney born Roman Catholic.' Twelve surviving children. Buried All Saints, West Barsham (per his own will, next to his wife). Elizabethan poet whose 600-poem commonplace book survives as Bodleian MS Tanner 175.
notables: 'Last member of the Gurney family to be born a Roman Catholic.' Godmother: Lady Catherine Howard. Twelve surviving children of thirteen begotten (per epitaph verse). Confirmed lord of West Barsham (held by one knight's fee of the manor of Castleacre), Great Ellingham (held of the heirs of Lord Bardolph), Irstead (held of the Bishop of Norwich), and Gurney's manor in Hingham (held of the heirs of Henry Lord Morley) by Francis Blomefield's parish surveys for 1572 (vols. i, ii, vii). Will of 1614 directed burial 'in the parish Church next to my wife there' (Ellen Blennerhasset, buried West Barsham), and warned his sons against holding 'fantasticall or erroneous opinions, so adjudged by our Bishop or civill Lawes.' Elizabethan poet, critic, and bibliophile rediscovered by Steven W. May in Spenser Studies 20 (2005). Tomb almost certainly at All Saints, West Barsham (not Great Ellingham as previously recorded); an epitaph verse 'Of Henry Gournay squire' was preserved in connection with Great Ellingham, his principal late-life residence, by Verily Anderson, Friends and Relations (1980), p. 21.
landHoldings: • West Barsham manor, Norfolk (primary family seat; hall burned 1815, 16th-c. north wing survives Grade II listed). • Great Ellingham manor (held from Bishop of Norwich). • Harpley manor, Norfolk (purchased 1587; presented to church 1588, 1602). • Irsted manor (held of Bishop of Norwich; sold to Sir Peter Gleane before 1632 by son/grandson). • Gurney's manor, Hingham (held of Henry Lord Morley). • West Barsham rectory (purchased from Thomas Fermor, Esq. for £100, 1595 — deed at Hunstanton Hall). • Advowson, third part of Attleborough church (presented 1581).

name: Anthony Gurney
dates: b. c. 1499 — d. 4 Jan. 1555/6 (per Blomefield, vol. vii)
geography: West Barsham Hall & Great Ellingham, Norfolk
summary: Boy lord of West Barsham (inherited c. 1508 aged about 9). BOLEYN CONNECTION: Second cousin of Queen Anne Boleyn through his Heydon mother. Brought Great Ellingham and the Lovell-Mortimer-of-Attleborough lands into the family by his marriage to Margaret Lovell. Foreman of the Norfolk grand jury that indicted the Earl of Surrey, January 1546/7.
notables: BOLEYN CONNECTION: Second cousin of QUEEN ANNE BOLEYN. Both were great-grandchildren of Sir Geoffrey Boleyn, Lord Mayor of London 1457–58: Anthony through Sir Geoffrey's daughter Anne Boleyn the elder of Blickling (who married Sir Henry Heydon of Baconsthorpe Castle, Anthony's maternal grandfather), Queen Anne Boleyn through Sir Geoffrey's son Sir William Boleyn. Married Margaret Lovell c. 1519 — daughter and coheir of Sir Robert Lovell by Ela Conyers. Sir Robert Lovell was 'cousin and coheir of Sir Thomas Lovell, privy counsellor to King Henry VII and Henry VIII and Knight of the Garter' (per Blomefield, vol. vii, pp. 42–47). Margaret's mother Ela Conyers was sister of Anne Conyers, mother of the antiquary Sir Henry Spelman of Congham (per Blomefield, vol. i, pp. 482–490) — making Anthony's children first cousins once removed of Spelman. Connected via the Heydon sisters to Sir William Paston of Caister, the Cobhams (and so to Sir Thomas Wyatt the poet via his wife Elizabeth Brooke), and the Lestranges of Hunstanton. Lord of West Barsham 'in 1514' per Blomefield. Foreman of the Norfolk grand jury that indicted Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, on 7 January 1546/7 — the indictment that led to Surrey's execution two weeks later. Died 4 January 1555/6 (Old Style 1555); his eldest son Francis (G16) had predeceased him, so his grandson Henry (G15) succeeded. 17th great-grandfather of Allen Gurney.
landHoldings: • Great Ellingham manor, Norfolk — acquired via marriage to Margaret Lovell (she and her sister co-heiresses of Sir Robert Lovell; through her mother of families Conyers of Finningham and Fitz-Ralf). • West Barsham manor, Norfolk (primary seat). • Irsted manor, Norfolk. • Manor of Hingham-Gurneys (ancient holding from Henry II period, held of heirs of Lords Bardolf).

name: William Gurney V
geography: West Barsham; Irstead, Norfolk; Baconsthorpe (Heydon connection)
summary: Eldest son and heir-apparent of William Gurney IV (G19); died before his father; married Anne Heydon of Baconsthorpe Castle, bringing direct descent from Anne Boleyn the elder of Blickling and the Heydon-Boleyn-Howard cousinage of late-medieval Norfolk into the family.
notables: Married Anne Heydon, daughter of Sir Henry Heydon (Privy Councillor to Henry VII and builder of Baconsthorpe Castle, English Heritage open free near Holt, Norfolk) and Anne Boleyn the elder of Blickling. Anne Boleyn the elder was sister of Sir William Boleyn, paternal grandfather of Queen Anne Boleyn — making William V's son Anthony G17 a second cousin of the queen. The marriage took place 'shortly after 28 May 1484' per modern Heydon scholarship reading Sir Henry Heydon's Prerogative Court of Canterbury will of 1503/4. Anne Heydon's siblings married into the Pastons of Caister, the Cobhams (and so to Sir Thomas Wyatt the poet), and the Lestranges of Hunstanton — the latter being the kinship that explains the appointment of William V's great-great-grandson Francis Gurney (G14) as financial agent to the Lestranges 1612–1636. Died vita patris before his father; widow Anne remarried Sir Lionel Dymoke of Ashby, Lincolnshire (d. 17 Aug. 1519), and died c. 1521. DG-Supp Note 132 provides the full IPM text (Escheats XIII Henry VIII, part 1, No. 103). Death: 16 February 1507/8. Grandson Anthony Gurnay heir, aged 30+. Son William junior predeceased him. Two trust deeds: (1) 19 September 1485 (2 Richard III) for Swathings/Hingham manors, feoffees including William Calthorpe Knt.; (2) 6 April 1505 (21 Henry VII) for West Barsham/Denver manors, feoffees including Edward Howard Knt. (future Lord Admiral). Cantley tenure: Swathings still held under the lords of Cantley — the old senior Gournay seat — 400 years after the senior line was established there.
landHoldings: • Irsted manor, Norfolk (primary documented holding). • Swathings manor in Hardingham, Norfolk — mesne lord under the senior Gournay line (documented from reign of Henry II per Daniel Gurney's Record). • Hingham-Gurneys manor.

name: William Gurney IV
summary: Son of Thomas Gournay II and Margaret Jerningham. Escheator for Norfolk; of council to the Duke of Norfolk in 1477. Married Anne Calthorpe, only daughter of Sir William Calthorpe KB of Burnham Thorpe by his first wife Elizabeth Grey. Died 18 January 1507/8 at Burnham Thorpe.
notables: Son of Thomas Gournay II and Margaret Jerningham. Escheator for Norfolk; of council to the Duke of Norfolk (John Howard) in 1477. Married Anne Calthorpe, daughter of Sir William Calthorpe, Knight of the Bath, of Burnham Thorpe (1410–1494), by his first wife Elizabeth Grey, daughter of Sir Reginald Grey, 3rd Baron Grey of Ruthyn. Anne Calthorpe is independently confirmed as Sir William Calthorpe's only daughter from his first marriage by at least eight non-Daniel-Gurney sources: Wikipedia, WikiTree (Calthorpe-7), Find a Grave #81101154, Geni, Lee-Warner's 'The Calthorps of Burnham' in Norfolk Archaeology IX (1884), Carr-Calthrop's Notes on the Families of Calthorpe & Calthrop (1933), Cotman & Meyrick's Engravings of Sepulchral Brasses in Norfolk (1838), and Sir William Calthorpe's full will printed in The East Anglian: Notes and Queries vol. ii p. 210. His 1507 will required 700 sheep to remain at West Barsham after his death — 'a considerable flock in those days,' as Daniel Gurney noted. Independently named as 'William Gournay, junior' receiving custody of the East Barsham manors of Roger Wood from John Earl of Oxford in 14 Henry VII (1499) by Francis Blomefield (History of Norfolk, vol. vii, pp. 53–65 — East Barsham parish entry). Died 18 January 1507/8 at Burnham Thorpe (his wife's home village, three centuries before Admiral Lord Nelson made the place famous). Lifetime spanned the entire Wars of the Roses (1455–85) and the first two Tudor decades.
landHoldings: • West Barsham manor, Norfolk. • Burnham Thorpe, Norfolk — died here (suggests land interest in this village, birthplace of Admiral Lord Nelson three centuries later). • Full manor holdings not individually documented in sources consulted; inherited the West Barsham and associated Norfolk portfolio from Thomas (Gen.20).

name: Thomas Gournay II
summary: Son of Thomas Gournay I and Catherine Kerville. Lord of West Barsham, Harpley, and Norwich. Married Margaret Jerningham of Somerleyton. Will dated 18 March 1469/70 (9 Edward IV) per Blomefield Vol. VIII, proved 27 July 1471.
notables: Son of Thomas Gournay I and Catherine Kerville. Married Margaret, daughter of Sir Thomas Jerningham, Knt., of Somerleyton, Suffolk — one of Norfolk and Suffolk's most powerful Catholic gentry families. Maintained three simultaneous gentry residences: West Barsham Hall, a house at Harpley, and a town house in St Gregory's parish, Norwich. His will, dated 18 March 1469/70 (9 Edward IV) and proved 27 July 1471, directed that he be buried in the chancel of Harpley church if he died at Harpley, or in the church of the Friars Minors (Greyfriars) at Norwich if he died there — independently confirmed by Francis Blomefield, History of Norfolk, vol. viii (1808), 'Freebridge Hundred and Half: Harpley,' pp. 452–459. The will left 'all the woollen and linen cloths' of the household to his wife Margaret as 'her own work and that of her servants' — rare first-person evidence of a 15th-century Norfolk gentry wife running a productive household textile operation. Died and was buried during the closing weeks of the Wars of the Roses.
landHoldings: • West Barsham manor, Norfolk (inherited from John, Gen.21). • Associated Norfolk manors from John's estate: Harpley, Hardingham, Loundhall in Saxthorpe, and the Heylesdon manors. • Specific deeds for Thomas not individually documented in sources consulted.

name: John de Gournay IV
summary: Mentioned in a deed of his uncle's, 1331. Father of Edmund Gurney (d.1387).
notables: Mentioned in a deed of his uncle John de Gournay II (Rector of Harpley), 1331. Father of Edmund Gurney, the lawyer who became steward of John of Gaunt's estates. Source: DG Record, Part I, pedigree p.286.
landHoldings: • Harpley manor, Norfolk (inherited from father John III). • Hardingham manor.

name: John de Gournay III
summary: Son of William III. Wife Jane de Lexham. Succeeded uncle John (Rector of Harpley) in 1332. Living 27 Edw. III (1353).
notables: Son of Sir William de Gournay III and Katherine de Baconsthorpe. Married Jane, daughter of Edmund de Lexham (married before 1324). Succeeded his uncle John de Gournay II, Rector and Patron of Harpley, who died in 1332. Living in 27 Edward III (1353). Source: DG Record, Part I, pedigree p.286.
landHoldings: • Harpley manor, Norfolk (succeeded uncle John, Rector of Harpley, in 1332). • Hardingham manor. • Swathings in Hardingham.

spouses.name: Jane de Lexham
spouses.notes: Daughter of Edmund de Lexham; married before 1324

name: Sir William de Gournay III, Knt.
summary: Married Katherine de Baconsthorpe. Sold all estates to brother John, Rector of Harpley, in 1294.
notables: 14 Edward I (1286). Married Katherine, daughter of Edmund Baconsthorpe. In 1294, sold for an annuity all his estates to his brother John de Gournay II, Priest, Rector and Patron of Harpley, who settled them on William's son John III. Sealed with an engrailed cross. Source: DG Record, Part I, pp.279, 286.
landHoldings: • Harpley manor (sold to brother John, 1294). • Hardingham manor. • Swathings in Hardingham.

spouses.name: Katherine de Baconsthorpe
spouses.notes: Daughter of Edmund Baconsthorpe

children.name: John de Gournay II
children.notes: Priest, Rector and Patron of Harpley; d. 1332. Received brother William's estates 1294. Buried Harpley chancel. COLLATERAL.

name: Sir John de Gournay I, Knt.
geography: Harpley, Norfolk; Lewes, Sussex; Holy Land
summary: Present at battles of Lewes (1264) and Evesham (1265). Accompanied Edward I to Holy Land 1270.
notables: Living 1245. Present at the battle of Lewes (1264) on the side of Sir Henry Hastings against Henry III, and at the battle of Evesham (1265). Estate seized by Earl Warren as a rebel. Presented by jury of Mitford in 1257 for not being knighted. Accompanied Prince Edward (later Edward I) to the Holy Land in 1270. Arms: Argent, a cross engrailed gules — borne by his descendants ever since. Source: DG Record, Part I, pp.279, 286; Blomefield, History of Norfolk. DG-Supp Note 112 preserves the full Latin text of the South Wootton plea (1264): livestock inventory of 3 horses, 4 oxen, 14 cows, 171 sheep seized because John 'was in the conflict of Lewes against the Lord King.' DG-Supp Note 114 gives the full Latin text of the Crusade letters of protection (Rot. Patent 54 Hen. III, 1270). Rotuli Hundredorum 1274 shows Harpley tenure chain: King → Earl Warren → Caletorp → Gournay.
landHoldings: • Harpley manor, Norfolk. • Hardingham manor. • Swathings in Hardingham.

name: William de Gournay II
summary: Son of Matthew de Gournay. Father of Sir John I. Living 1234 and 1243.
notables: Son of Matthew de Gournay and Rose de Burnham. Living 1234 and 1243 per pedigree. Father of Sir John de Gournay I. Source: DG Record, Part I, pedigree p.286. DG-Supp Note 111: William witnessed a charter of William de Clifford to the Abbey of Dore, Herefordshire, in 1220 (Dodsworth MS. 42, Bodleian Library).
landHoldings: • Harpley manor, Norfolk (inherited from father Matthew). • Hardingham/Swathings.

spouses.name: Katherine
spouses.notes: DG-I pedigree calls her 'probably a Baconsthorpe.' DG-Supp Note 113 (1858) proposes she was an Ingoldesthorpe, based on a fine at DG-I p. 325. The two identifications are unresolved — they may represent the same woman (with the Supplement being DG's later, more considered opinion) or two different Katherines in successive generations (G28 and G26).

name: Matthew de Gournay
summary: Married Rose de Burnham c.1183. Acquired Gurney's manor in Harpley through her.
notables: Son of William de Gournay I. Hameline Plantagenet, Earl Warren, gave in marriage his kinswoman Rose, daughter and heir of Reginald de Burnham (Fitz-Philip), about the year 1183. Through Rose he acquired Gurney's manor in Harpley, Norfolk. Gave tithes of Hardingham to the church (Harl. MSS. 970). Held manor of Swathings in Hardingham. Source: DG Record, Part I, pp.278-279, 286; Blomefield, History of Norfolk (Harpley). DG Supplement Note 109 corrects the main text: Matthew was living in 1217 (Fine Roll 2 Henry III), paying 20 marks for a writ of attaint concerning his tenement of Swathings.
landHoldings: • Gurney's manor in Harpley, Norfolk (acquired through marriage to Rose de Burnham c.1183). • Swathings manor in Hardingham. • Runhall.

spouses.name: Rose de Burnham
spouses.notes: Daughter and heir of Reginald Fitz-Philip/de Burnham; given in marriage by Hameline Earl Warren c.1183. Burnhams were a younger branch of the house of Warren.

name: William de Gournay I
summary: Knight. Lord of Runhall and Swathings. Held Montigny-sur-Andelle in Normandy in parage — proof of blood descent from Barons of Gournay.
notables: Son of Walter de Gournay. Knight (designated 'Dominus Willelmus de Gurney'). Lord of Runhall and Swathings in Hardingham, Norfolk. Held in capite the lordship of Montigny-sur-Andelle in the Pays de Bray, Normandy — parcel of the great fief of the Lords of Gournay, held in parage (equal tenure). This Norman holding constitutes 'incontestable proof of his descent in blood from the Barons of Gournay' (DG Record, Part I, p.278). Living 1167. Source: DG Record, Part I, pp.277-278, 286; Liber Niger Scaccarii.
landHoldings: • Runhall manor, Norfolk. • Swathings manor in Hardingham, Norfolk. • Montigny-sur-Andelle, Normandy (held in parage from the Dukes of Normandy).

name: Walter de Gournay
summary: Lord of manors in Norfolk and Suffolk. Ancestor of the entire Norfolk junior branch. Confirmed as Gournay blood by a French royal court.
notables: JUNCTION POINT — JUNIOR NORFOLK BRANCH. Youngest son of Gerard de Gournay (Crusader) and Edith de Warenne. Lived during the civil wars of the reign of Stephen (1135-1154). Held lands in Suffolk under Manasser de Dampmartin (Liber Niger Scaccarii, vol. i, p.298). Ancestor of the entire Norfolk junior Gournay line from which the West Barsham Gurneys, the banking Gurneys, and through Francis Gurney's son John, the American Gurneys descend. His elder brother Hugh IV continued the senior Norman baron line. Source: DG Record, Part I, pp.277-278, 286.
landHoldings: • Lands in Suffolk held under Manasser de Dampmartin (Liber Niger Scaccarii). • Norfolk manors (Runhall, Swathings in Hardingham) — held as mesne lords under the Barons of Gournay.

label: Norman Barons of England — Post-Conquest Settlement

name: Gerard de Gournay
summary: CRUSADER. Married Edith de Warenne. Joined First Crusade 1096, died Holy Land.
notables: CRUSADER. Married Edith de Warenne (d/o William de Warenne, 1st Earl of Surrey — ~£57bn Domesday equivalent). Joined First Crusade 1096, captured Jerusalem July 1099. Died Holy Land. Daughter Gundred: patroness of Byland Abbey & Rievaulx Abbey, Yorkshire.
landHoldings: • Caister, Norfolk (English holdings documented). • Gournay-en-Bray seigneury and surrounding Pays de Bray, Normandy. • Lessingham Priory, Norfolk — founded, attached to Abbey of Bec. • Cantley, Norfolk — documented holding. • Norfolk manors inherited from Hugh III (Gen.27) then expanded through Edith de Warenne marriage connection.

spouses.name: Edith de Warenne
spouses.notes: Daughter of William de Warenne, 1st Earl of Surrey (~£57bn Domesday equivalent)

children.name: Hugh de Gournay IV
children.notes: Eldest son. SENIOR BARON LINE (not Allen's direct line). See related entry.

children.name: Walter de Gournay
children.notes: G31 in direct line. Youngest son. Ancestor of the entire Norfolk junior branch.

children.name: Gundred de Gournay
children.notes: Married Nigel de Albini 1118. Patroness of Byland Abbey & Rievaulx Abbey.

name: Hugh de Gournay IV (Senior Baron Line)
summary: SENIOR BARON LINE — not in Allen's direct ancestry. Eldest son of Gerard. The direct line passes through his younger brother Walter.
notables: Raised at court of Henry I. Married (1) Beatrix de Vermandois (Carolingian/Charlemagne royal descent); (2) Melisende de Coucy. Founded Clairruissel Priory. Captured 1173 during Henry the Young King's rebellion.
landHoldings: • Three knights' fees in Norfolk (documented Pipe Rolls). • Manors in Buckinghamshire, Bedfordshire, and Oxfordshire (Red Book of the Exchequer). • Gournay-en-Bray seigneury, Normandy — the ancestral fortress town. • Clairruissel Priory, Normandy — founded with second wife Melisende de Coucy.

spouses.name: Beatrix de Vermandois
spouses.notes: Carolingian/Charlemagne royal descent; first wife

spouses.name: Melisende de Coucy
spouses.notes: Second wife; co-founder of Clairruissel Priory

name: Hugh de Gournay V (Senior Baron Line)
summary: SENIOR BARON LINE — not in Allen's direct ancestry. Son of Hugh IV. Last of the senior Norman baron line. Main line extinct; junior Norfolk branch continued.
notables: Last of the main Norman baron line. Founded Bellosanne Abbey, Normandy (1198). Vacillated between English and French allegiance when John lost Normandy (1204). Died Rouen Oct. 1214. Main Norman line extinct. Junior Norfolk branch continued.
landHoldings: • Flegg, Norfolk (English manors). • Manors in Oxfordshire, Buckinghamshire, and Bedfordshire (documented in Curia Regis Rolls and Testa de Nevill). • Confirmed by Richard I's 1200 charter confirming his holdings. • Norman territory (great fief/honour of Bray, including Gournay-en-Bray fortress) — lost when Philip Augustus expelled the English from Normandy in 1204. • Bellosanne Abbey, Normandy — founded 1198.

children.name: Gurney [name not yet established]
children.notes: G23 in direct line via junior Norfolk branch

name: Hugh de Gournay III
summary: Lord of Gournay-en-Bray. Norman knight. Buried Abbey of Bec, Normandy.
notables: Added twenty-four villages to the Gournay lordship. Battle of Hastings. Received English manors as Conquest reward. Previously sailed to England c.1035 for Edward the Confessor. Witnessed William I's Caen charters 1077 & 1082. Buried Abbey of Bec, Normandy (ruins survive near Brionne).
landHoldings: • Liston, Essex (Domesday 1086 — held directly of the king). • Fordham, Essex (Domesday 1086). • Ardleigh, Essex (Domesday 1086). • Norfolk manors (granted post-Conquest, specific parcels documented in Daniel Gurney's Record as chiefly in Norfolk and Suffolk). • Gournay-en-Bray fortress town and the Norman honour of Bray. • Abbey of Bec, Normandy — endowed and buried here.

name: Hugh de Gournay II
summary: 'The Fortifier.' Fought at Battle of Mortemer 1054.
notables: Fought at Battle of Mortemer (1054) — one of three principal Norman commanders. Charter witness to Duke William from c.1060. Nicknamed 'The Fortifier' — built Gournay's triple wall, double ditch and tower. Possibly died from wounds at Cardiff c.1074.
landHoldings: • Gournay-en-Bray seigneury — the walled fortress town and surrounding Pays de Bray territory. • 'The Fortifier': built triple wall, double ditch, and tower at Gournay — major investment in the property as a defensive stronghold on the eastern Norman frontier. • No English holdings — pre-Conquest.

name: Renaud de Gournay
summary: Held seigneury of Gournay. Charter 989–996 confirms his existence.
notables: Held seigneury of Gournay. Son Gautier de la Ferté founded priory of La Ferté-en-Bray (charter 989-996 names Renaud and his wife Alberade — primary source confirmation of Renaud's existence).
landHoldings: • Gournay-en-Bray seigneury, Pays de Bray, Normandy. • La Ferté-en-Bray priory — endowed by son Gautier citing father Renaud.

spouses.name: Alberade
spouses.notes: Named in charter 989–996 for La Ferté-en-Bray priory

name: Hugh de Gournay I
summary: Son of Eudes. First lord born in Gournay.
notables: Son of Eudes. First lord born in Gournay. First generation to know no homeland but Normandy.
landHoldings: • Gournay-en-Bray seigneury — inherited from Eudes.

name: Eudes (Odon) de Gournay
summary: ORIGIN OF THE LINE. Viking companion of Rollo. ~37 generations to Allen.
notables: ORIGIN OF THE LINE. Viking warrior, companion of ROLLO. At Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte (911) Rollo received Normandy from Frankish King Charles the Simple. Eudes received the Pays de Bray as his portion. Daniel Gurney acknowledged: 'the existence of Eudes... is a matter of tradition' — no contemporary document survives. From Eudes to Allen Gurney: ~37 generations, ~1,160 years.
landHoldings: • Gournay-en-Bray and the Pays de Bray, Normandy — granted by Rollo c.911-912 as the founding land grant of the entire Gurney family story. • The town of Gournay-en-Bray survives today in Seine-Maritime, Normandy (~50 miles east of Rouen). 12th-century Collegiate Church of Saint-Hildevert still stands. • This single land grant initiated a documented property-holding lineage lasting ~750 years (911 to 1661 when the West Barsham Gurneys became extinct in the direct male line in England).

label: End of Known Record — The Wall of History

name: Unknown Scandinavian ancestors
summary: WALL OF KNOWABLE HISTORY. Eudes's Norse ancestry entirely unrecorded.
notables: WALL OF KNOWABLE HISTORY. Eudes ancestory may parallel that of Rollo given that Eudes was reportedly a companion of Rollo with Norse ancestry (Norse earls of Møre, Norway). Eudes's own parentage and Norse clan are entirely unrecorded. The Gurney male line disappears into the unrecorded Norse world of the 9th century.
landHoldings: • Unknown. No Scandinavian land records attributable to Eudes's ancestors survive.
